newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines unit's board resigns.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines unit's board resigns.

text.p: The board of directors of ailing Canadian Airlines International Ltd. resigned on Friday in a move the carrier's unions called a tactic to pressure employees into accepting controversial wage cuts.

Parent company Canadian Airlines Corp. said the Canadian Airlines International board, which included AMR Corp. Chairman Robert Crandall and Don Carty, president of AMR unit American Airlines, resigned on the advice of lawyers to avoid personal financial liability.

The board of Canadian Airlines Corp. remained unchanged and Canadian Airlines International's affairs were to be directed by the parent company and Aurora Airline Investments Inc., a holding company AMR set up for its 33 percent investment in Canadian Airlines.

Calling the move a "gimmick," Buzz Hargrove, president of the Canadian Auto Workers union, said the flight of CAI's directors was part of a master plan by Canadian Airlines Chief Executive Kevin Benson to pressure workers into taking the 10 percent wage cut.

"It's designed to create uncertainty in the minds of the workers and it's having some success with the minority," Hargrove said, adding the CAW, which represents 3,700 workers at Canadian, continued to call for government re-regulation of the domestic airline industry and a rejection of pay cuts.

The rollbacks are one of three main parts of the company's survival plan, which also includes major route restructurings and a call for a C$48 million ($36 million) reduction in service fees paid annually to Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR.
Canadian, which devised the strategy to stave off a financial collapse that it says could come early next year, set a Nov. 30 deadline for all participants to respond.
Despite the union charges, Canadian said the 10 directors, eight of whom continue to serve on the parent company's board, resigned at the urging of their lawyers, not the company's management.

"There was no particular event at our end that triggered this," Canadian spokeswoman Claudia Cattaneo said. "The reality is that the board at this stage felt that the personal exposure to them for remaining on the board of our operating company is great."

Bob Rae, adviser to the International Association of Machinists, the biggest union at Canadian, and a former premier of Ontario, criticised the timing of the move, which came after a meeting this week between Benson and the unions to explore alternative ideas for the carrier's survival.

"I regret that they felt the need to take that kind of a decision at this stage in the proceedings. I would have thought that people (directors) might have wanted to wait until negotiations really started in earnest...to maintain confidence in the company," Rae told CBC Radio in Vancouver.
Friday's resignations were unlikely to affect the day-to-day opperations of the airline, said Ted Larkin, analyst with Bunting Warburg in Toronto.
